planting.note: Direct sow every few weeks from early spring through late summer for a continuous supply; the purple-pink shank color intensifies with cool weather and full sun exposure.

directions: Apache is a fast-growing open-pollinated scallion selected for shanks that flush from rosy purple to a deeper wine color as the plant matures, set off nicely against slender blue-green tops. Sow thickly in shallow drills and thin as needed, since it is typically pulled young for salads, garnishes, and quick pickles rather than grown to full onion size. Flavor is mild and sweet compared with many bunching types, making it popular raw. Because it germinates and bulks up quickly in cool conditions, succession sowing every two to three weeks keeps a steady harvest through spring and fall.
sources: Specialty seed catalog variety descriptions (e.g. Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, Kitazawa Seed Company)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or sow in late summer for an overwintered crop where winters are mild; deep red shank color develops best under cool fall or spring conditions.

directions: Crimson Forest is a Japanese-type bunching onion whose slender, non-bulbing stalks stain a deep garnet-red at the base, holding that color well even after cooking, which sets it apart visually from standard green scallions. It clumps and regrows from a fibrous root system rather than forming a bulb, so a single sowing can be cut repeatedly as new shoots emerge. Flavor is crisp and mildly pungent, good raw in salads or as a colorful garnish, and it holds up reasonably well through short cold snaps. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart for straight, uniform stalks and keep beds evenly moist for tender texture.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension -- Growing Onions

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer; White Spear was selected to resist bulbing, splitting, and leaf-curl through hot summer weather better than most bunching types.

directions: White Spear produces tall, straight, blue-green tops over long, cylindrical white shanks that stay uniform and resist the splitting and curling that plague many bunching onions during peak summer heat. It is less winter-hardy than overwintering types such as Evergreen Hardy White, so it performs best sown for a spring-through-fall harvest window rather than left to stand through hard freezes. Its clean, uniform stalks and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for a continuous summer scallion supply. Harvest at pencil thickness for the mildest flavor and most tender texture, or let shanks thicken slightly for a stronger bite.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange catalog description

planting.note: Sow in mid- to late summer for overwintering and an early spring harvest, or sow in early spring for a summer crop; mulch overwintered plantings in the coldest zones.

directions: Guardsman resulted from breeding between bunching and bulb onion types, combining a vigorous root system and thicker, milder shank with the non-bulbing habit of a scallion. It was bred specifically to survive cold winters when sown in late summer, resuming growth early the following spring ahead of most other bunching cultivars. The larger tops and root vigor also make it a strong performer for a standard spring or summer sowing. Because it is milder than many bunching onions, it suits fresh eating as well as light cooking, and clumps can be divided to extend a planting.
sources: J.W. Jung Seed Company catalog description

common_name: Curly Blue Chives (Twisted-Leaf Ornamental German Garlic)

planting.note: Set container plants or divisions in spring or early fall in gritty, sharply drained soil; this dwarf form of German garlic is grown chiefly for its twisted, steel-blue foliage rather than for the kitchen.

directions: This dwarf, glaucous-leaved form of German garlic forms tight tussocks of narrow foliage that twists into distinctive curls as it matures, staying attractive well before and after its rounded pink-lilac flower heads appear in late summer. It thrives in the same lean, fast-draining conditions favored by other rock garden and trough plants, and resents heavy, waterlogged soil more than most culinary alliums. Established clumps are notably drought tolerant once rooted in and rarely need division for vigor, though lifting and splitting every few years is an easy way to propagate more plants. While technically edible like the species, it is grown almost exclusively as a compact, long-blooming edging or container ornamental rather than a culinary crop.
sources: specialty perennial nursery cultivar records (e.g. Plant Delights Nursery, Digging Dog Nursery)
